mistakes.fix: Think of curling the chest down towards the pelvis.

safety: Avoid if loaded spinal flexion aggravates a back condition.
Protect your knees with padding on hard floors.
checks: Check the rope is secure and the pin fully inserted.
Place a pad under the knees.
reduceLoad: Reduce the weight when your hips sit back, your arms start pulling or you feel it mostly in the hip flexors or lower back.

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Pick a load you could manage for about 20 reps while learning to curl the spine.
programming.judgeLoad: Feel a strong abdominal contraction each rep and stop at one to two reps in reserve.
programming.progression: Double progression: build to the top of the rep range, then add one plate.
programming.increase: Increase the weight when every set hits the top of the rep range without the hips moving. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the load if the hips start sitting back, and reduce it if the lower back aches.

name: Machine crunch
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis. Secondary: internal and external obliques.

steps.start: Sit in the ab crunch machine with your back against the pad, feet under the foot rollers and hands on the handles or chest pads.
steps.setup: Adjust the seat so the pivot of the machine lines up roughly with your mid-torso and the chest pads or handles sit at shoulder level; select a light weight.
steps.feet: Hook your feet under the rollers or place them on the footplate, knees bent at about 90 degrees.
steps.grip: Hold the handles beside your head or rest your forearms on the pads, depending on the model; keep the arm position fixed.
steps.posture: Sit tall with your back on the pad and your chest up at the start.
steps.brace: Brace your abs and pull your ribs down slightly before the first rep.
steps.initiate: Start by curling your chest down towards your pelvis rather than pulling with your arms.
steps.concentric: Crunch forwards until your torso is fully flexed and the abs are tightly contracted.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you crunch, inhale as you return.
steps.eccentric: Return slowly to the upright position, letting your abs stretch without the weight stack touching down.
steps.rom: Use the machine's full arc as long as the movement comes from the spine and not the hips or arms.
steps.tempo: 1-1-2-0: one second in, one-second squeeze, two seconds back.
steps.finish: Return to the upright start with a little tension still on the stack.
steps.exit: Let the weight down gently, release the handles and lift your feet out of the rollers.

cues: Keep the stack off the rest

mistakes.m: Pulling with the arms or shoulders.
mistakes.fix: Relax the arms and imagine the pads are fixed to your chest.

mistakes.m: Using the hip flexors to fold at the hips.
mistakes.fix: Lower the weight and focus on rounding the spine.

mistakes.m: Letting the weight crash between reps.
mistakes.fix: Use a two-second return and stop short of the stack.

mistakes.m: Seat set too high or low so the pivot feels awkward.
mistakes.fix: Adjust until the curl feels smooth and centred on your abs.

safety: Avoid if loaded spinal flexion aggravates a back condition.
Do not jerk heavy loads; smooth reps protect the back and neck.
checks: Check the seat height and pin are locked.
Confirm the selected weight before you start.
reduceLoad: Reduce the weight when you need to pull with the arms, lift your hips or rush the return.

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with a weight you could do about 20 times.
programming.judgeLoad: Each rep should be a controlled curl with one or two reps left at the end of the set.
programming.progression: Double progression: add reps, then move the pin down one plate.
programming.increase: Increase the load when all sets reach the top of the rep range with full control. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the load if you rely on the arms, and reduce it if your back complains.

name: Hanging knee raise
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas. Secondary: obliques, rectus femoris, forearm flexors, latissimus dorsi.

steps.start: Hang from a pull-up bar with straight arms, feet off the floor and legs hanging straight.
steps.setup: Use a sturdy pull-up bar high enough that your feet clear the floor; use a box to reach it if needed.
steps.feet: Keep your legs together and let them hang still before starting.
steps.grip: Grip the bar overhand about shoulder-width, fully wrapping your thumbs; straps can help if grip fails first.
steps.posture: Pull your shoulders slightly down away from your ears and keep the chest open without swinging.
steps.brace: Brace your abs and slightly tuck your pelvis to remove any arch in the lower back.
steps.initiate: Begin by tilting the pelvis backwards, then bring the knees up.
steps.concentric: Raise your knees towards your chest, curling the pelvis up so the tailbone tucks under at the top.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you lift, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Lower your legs slowly until they are straight below you, without swinging backwards.
steps.rom: Lift until your thighs pass parallel and the pelvis curls up; lower to a full hang.
steps.tempo: 1-1-2-0: one second up, brief pause, two seconds down.
steps.finish: Finish each rep in a still hang before starting the next.
steps.exit: Lower to a still hang, then place your feet on the box or drop softly to the floor with bent knees.

mistakes.m: Swinging and using momentum.
mistakes.fix: Pause in a dead hang between reps and slow the lowering.

mistakes.m: Only lifting the knees to hip height without curling the pelvis.
mistakes.fix: Think of bringing your belt buckle towards your chin.

mistakes.m: Shrugging the shoulders up to the ears.
mistakes.fix: Pull the shoulders down to engage the lats before each rep.

mistakes.m: Grip giving out before the abs.
mistakes.fix: Use straps or ab slings, or move to the captain's chair.

safety: Avoid if hanging hurts your shoulders; use the captain's chair instead.
Step down from the bar rather than dropping if you are tired.
checks: Check the bar is secure and can take your weight.
Use a stable box or step to reach the bar.
reduceLoad: Reduce reps or switch to a regression when you start swinging, cannot curl the pelvis or your grip fails first.

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with as many controlled reps as you can do without swinging.
programming.judgeLoad: Stop the set when you need to swing or cannot tuck the pelvis.
programming.progression: Add reps, then add a pause at the top, then hold a light dumbbell between the feet.
programming.increase: Increase difficulty once you manage 15 strict reps for all sets. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep reps steady if swinging creeps in, and reduce if the shoulders ache.

name: Hanging leg raise
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas, rectus femoris. Secondary: obliques, forearm flexors, latissimus dorsi.

steps.start: Hang from a pull-up bar with straight arms, legs straight and together, feet clear of the floor.
steps.setup: Use a bar high enough for your straight legs to hang without touching the floor.
steps.feet: Keep your legs straight and together with the feet pointed or relaxed.
steps.grip: Overhand grip about shoulder-width with thumbs wrapped; use straps if grip limits you.
steps.posture: Draw the shoulders down and keep the body still in a hollow hang.
steps.brace: Brace hard and tuck the pelvis slightly before each rep.
steps.initiate: Begin by tilting the pelvis back, then lift the straight legs forwards.
steps.concentric: Raise your straight legs until they are at least parallel to the floor, ideally higher, curling the pelvis up at the top.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you lift, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Lower your straight legs slowly to the hang, keeping them from swinging behind you.
steps.rom: Lift to at least hip height with straight legs; higher with a pelvic curl is the goal.
steps.tempo: 1-1-3-0: one second up, brief pause, three seconds down.
steps.finish: Return to a still hang before the next rep.
steps.exit: Step down onto a box or drop softly with bent knees.

mistakes.m: Bending the knees to make it easier.
mistakes.fix: Keep the legs straight; regress to knee raises if needed.

mistakes.m: Swinging into each rep.
mistakes.fix: Start from a still hang and lower slowly.

mistakes.m: Lifting only with the hip flexors and arching the back.
mistakes.fix: Tuck the pelvis first and finish with a curl.

mistakes.m: Grip fatigue limiting the set.
mistakes.fix: Use straps or ab slings.

safety: Avoid if hanging aggravates your shoulders.
Hamstring tightness can limit range; do not force the legs higher by arching.
checks: Check the bar is secure.
Use a box to mount and dismount safely.
reduceLoad: Return to knee raises when you cannot keep the legs straight, start swinging or the lower back arches.

programming.frequency: 2 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with the number of strict straight-leg reps you can do; use knee raises if under five.
programming.judgeLoad: End each set when straight legs or a still hang can no longer be kept.
programming.progression: Add reps, then increase height, then add ankle weight.
programming.increase: Increase difficulty when you complete 12 strict reps. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the same if swinging appears, and reduce if shoulders or lower back ache.

name: Captain's chair knee raise
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas. Secondary: obliques, rectus femoris.

steps.start: Step up onto the captain's chair, rest your forearms on the arm pads, grip the handles and let your legs hang with your back against the pad.
steps.setup: Use a vertical knee-raise station with a back pad and forearm rests; check the pads are firm and the frame stable.
steps.feet: Let your legs hang straight and together below you.
steps.grip: Forearms along the pads, hands gripping the handles, elbows directly under your shoulders.
steps.posture: Press your back into the pad and push down through the forearms so your shoulders do not shrug up.
steps.brace: Brace your abs and keep your lower back against the pad.
steps.initiate: Begin by tilting the pelvis back, then lift the knees.
steps.concentric: Bring your knees up towards your chest, curling the pelvis off the pad at the top.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you lift, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Lower your legs slowly to the hanging start without swinging.
steps.rom: Raise until your thighs are above parallel with the pelvis curled; lower until legs are straight.
steps.tempo: 1-1-2-0: one second up, pause, two seconds down.
steps.finish: Return to a still hang before the next rep.
steps.exit: Lower your legs, place your feet on the steps and step down.

mistakes.m: Swinging the legs.
mistakes.fix: Pause at the bottom of each rep.

mistakes.m: Lifting only to hip height.
mistakes.fix: Curl the pelvis up off the pad at the top.

mistakes.m: Shrugging into the pads.
mistakes.fix: Push the forearms down to lift the chest.

safety: Avoid if the position aggravates your shoulders.
Step down carefully; do not jump from the station.
checks: Check the station is stable and the pads are firm.
Make sure the steps are dry.
reduceLoad: Reduce reps when you start swinging or feel mainly hip flexors or the lower back.

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Begin with controlled bodyweight reps.
programming.judgeLoad: End the set with one to two clean reps left.
programming.progression: Add reps, then a pause, then straighten the legs or hold a dumbbell between the feet.
programming.increase: Increase difficulty once 15 controlled reps are easy. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep reps the same if swinging appears.

name: Ab-wheel rollout
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis. Secondary: obliques, latissimus dorsi, anterior deltoid, triceps long head, hip flexors.

steps.start: Kneel on a mat with the ab wheel on the floor under your shoulders, holding both handles with straight arms.
steps.setup: Use a mat or pad for your knees and a wheel that rolls smoothly. A wall in front can limit range while learning.
steps.feet: Knees hip-width apart, toes tucked or flat; for the standing progression, feet hip-width.
steps.grip: Overhand grip on both handles, arms straight but not locked hard.
steps.posture: Round your back very slightly and tuck your pelvis, keeping the ribs pulled down.
steps.brace: Brace hard as if bracing for a punch and squeeze your glutes.
steps.initiate: Push the wheel forwards slowly, letting your hips and shoulders move forwards together.
steps.concentric: Pull the wheel back towards your knees by driving the hands down and back, keeping the hips tucked.
steps.breathing: Inhale on the way out, exhale as you roll back.
steps.eccentric: Roll out slowly while keeping the ribs down and the lower back from arching.
steps.rom: Roll out only as far as you can without your lower back sagging; progress to near full extension over time.
steps.tempo: 3-0-2-0: three seconds out, two seconds back.
steps.finish: Return to the start with hips over knees.
steps.exit: Place the wheel down, sit back onto your heels and stand up.

cues: Roll out only as far as you control

mistakes.m: Lower back sagging at full extension.
mistakes.fix: Shorten the range or use a wall stop.

mistakes.m: Leading with the hips on the way back.
mistakes.fix: Pull with the arms and abs, keeping the hips tucked.

mistakes.m: Rolling too far too soon.
mistakes.fix: Increase range gradually over weeks.

safety: Avoid if you have low-back pain with extension.
The standing rollout is advanced; build up from knees.
checks: Check the wheel rolls freely and handles are secure.
Use a pad under the knees.
reduceLoad: Reduce range when the lower back sags, you cannot return without hips leading or you feel pain.

programming.frequency: 2 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with a short range from your knees.
programming.judgeLoad: Each rep should finish with your lower back still neutral.
programming.progression: Increase range, then reps, then move to standing rollouts.
programming.increase: Increase range when 12 smooth reps are possible. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep range if the back sags.

name: Stability-ball crunch
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis. Secondary: internal and external obliques, transversus abdominis.

steps.start: Sit on a stability ball, walk your feet forwards and lie back until the ball supports your lower and mid back.
steps.setup: Use a ball sized so your thighs are roughly parallel to the floor when seated (often 55-65 cm); check it is fully inflated.
steps.feet: Feet flat, wider than hip-width for balance, knees bent at about 90 degrees.
steps.grip: Hands lightly behind your head, crossed over your chest, or holding a light plate at the chest later.
steps.posture: Let your back drape over the ball so the spine starts slightly extended, head supported by your hands.
steps.brace: Brace gently and keep the hips still so the ball does not roll.
steps.initiate: Begin by drawing your ribs towards your pelvis.
steps.concentric: Curl your upper body up until your torso is roughly upright, keeping the hips level.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Lower back over the ball slowly, letting the abs stretch.
steps.rom: Move from a gentle stretch over the ball to a full curl; the extra range is the benefit.
steps.tempo: 2-1-2-0: two seconds up, one-second squeeze, two seconds down.
steps.finish: Return to the stretched start with the hips still level.
steps.exit: Sit up, roll the ball back underneath you and stand up.

mistakes.m: Pulling on the head.
mistakes.fix: Use fingertips only or cross the arms.

mistakes.m: Feet too close and losing balance.
mistakes.fix: Widen the stance.

mistakes.m: Hips rising and falling with each rep.
mistakes.fix: Keep the hips level and move only the trunk.

safety: Use a ball rated for your weight; avoid worn balls.
If extending over the ball irritates your back, reduce the stretch.
checks: Inflate the ball properly and check for damage.
Clear space around you.
reduceLoad: Reduce range or reps when balance fails or you pull with your neck.

programming.rehab: A gentle range can be part of later-stage rehab if a physiotherapist approves.
programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with bodyweight.
programming.judgeLoad: End each set with one or two clean reps left.
programming.progression: Add reps, then hold a light plate.
programming.increase: Increase once 20 reps feel easy. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep it the same if you pull the neck.

name: Decline sit-up
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas. Secondary: obliques, rectus femoris.

steps.start: Lie back on a decline or slant board with your feet hooked under the rollers, knees bent and hands crossed on your chest.
steps.setup: Set the slant board to a moderate decline (15-30 degrees); steeper is harder. Check the foot rollers are locked.
steps.feet: Hook both feet under the rollers with knees bent.
steps.grip: Cross your arms on your chest or place fingertips by your temples.
steps.posture: Start lying on the board with a neutral spine and chin slightly tucked.
steps.brace: Brace your abs before lifting.
steps.initiate: Curl your head and shoulders up first, then continue lifting the trunk.
steps.concentric: Sit all the way up until your torso is upright or slightly past vertical, curling smoothly.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you sit up, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Lower back down slowly, uncurling one vertebra at a time.
steps.rom: Full sit-up from lying to upright; stop just short of resting fully if you want to keep tension.
steps.tempo: 2-0-2-0: two seconds up, two seconds down.
steps.finish: Finish upright, then begin lowering.
steps.exit: After the last rep, sit up, unhook your feet and step off the board.

mistakes.m: Jerking up with momentum.
mistakes.fix: Slow down and reduce the decline angle.

mistakes.m: Pulling on the neck.
mistakes.fix: Cross your arms on your chest.

mistakes.m: Dropping back quickly.
mistakes.fix: Lower for two to three seconds, uncurling one segment at a time.

mistakes.m: Pulling hard with the feet so the hip flexors do all the work.
mistakes.fix: Curl the ribs first, then sit up.

safety: Avoid if repeated loaded spinal flexion aggravates your back.
Lock the feet securely so you do not slip off the board.
Sit up before stepping off to avoid dizziness.
checks: Check the decline angle pin is secure.
Lock the foot rollers.
reduceLoad: Reduce the angle or reps when you need momentum, pull with the neck or feel it in the lower back.

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start on a gentle decline.
programming.judgeLoad: End with one or two clean reps left.
programming.progression: Add reps, then steeper angle, then hold a plate.
programming.increase: Increase difficulty once 15 controlled reps are easy. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the same if momentum creeps in.

name: Bicycle crunches
musclesText: Primary: external and internal obliques, rectus abdominis. Secondary: iliopsoas, rectus femoris.

steps.start: Lie on your back on a mat with fingertips behind your ears, shoulders lifted slightly and knees bent at 90 degrees over your hips.
steps.setup: Only a mat is needed.
steps.feet: Start with both knees over the hips and feet off the floor.
steps.grip: Fingertips lightly behind your head, elbows wide.
steps.posture: Lower back pressed into the mat, shoulder blades just off the floor.
steps.brace: Brace to keep the lower back down throughout.
steps.initiate: Rotate one shoulder towards the opposite knee while extending the other leg.
steps.concentric: Bring the right elbow towards the left knee while straightening the right leg, then switch sides.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you rotate, inhale as you switch.
steps.eccentric: Return through the centre slowly before rotating to the other side.
steps.rom: Rotate until the shoulder crosses towards the knee; extend the leg only as low as you keep the back flat.
steps.tempo: Slow, controlled: one second each side.
steps.finish: Each side counts as one rep.
steps.exit: Lower your feet and head to the mat.

mistakes.m: Moving fast and flapping the elbows.
mistakes.fix: Slow down and rotate from the ribcage, moving the shoulder towards the knee.

mistakes.m: Pulling on the head.
mistakes.fix: Keep fingertips light behind the ears.

mistakes.m: Lower back arching as the leg extends.
mistakes.fix: Keep the extended leg higher.

mistakes.m: Only touching elbow to knee without rotating.
mistakes.fix: Lift the shoulder blade and turn the chest.

safety: Stop if your neck strains; keep the hands light behind the head.
Avoid if repeated twisting in flexion aggravates your back.
Keep the extended leg high enough that your lower back stays on the mat.
checks: Use a mat.
Clear space for your legs.
reduceLoad: Reduce reps or keep the legs higher when your back arches or neck strains.

programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with bodyweight and slow reps.
programming.judgeLoad: Every rep should be slow and controlled with the lower back flat.
programming.progression: Add reps, then add a one-second pause at each side, then extend the legs lower.
programming.increase: Increase when 20 slow reps per side feel easy. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the same reps if your form slips or your neck strains.

name: Mountain climbers
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas. Secondary: anterior deltoid, quadriceps, cardiovascular system.

steps.start: Start in a high plank with your hands flat under your shoulders, arms straight and body in a line from head to heels.
steps.setup: No equipment is needed; use a non-slip floor or mat that will not slide under your hands. Have a timer ready for intervals.
steps.feet: Feet hip-width apart on the balls of the feet; the feet move alternately and land lightly under the hips each time.
steps.grip: Hands flat and shoulder-width, fingers spread, pushing the floor away so the upper back does not sag between the shoulder blades.
steps.posture: Keep the hips level with the shoulders and the neck neutral, gaze just ahead of your hands; shoulders stay stacked over the wrists.
steps.brace: Brace your abs and squeeze your glutes so the hips do not bounce or pike as the legs move.
steps.initiate: Drive one knee towards your chest, keeping the hips low and the shoulders over the hands.
steps.concentric: Alternate legs, driving each knee towards the chest as the other foot returns to the plank, at a pace you can control.
steps.breathing: Breathe rhythmically, roughly one breath per two or four knee drives; do not hold your breath.
steps.eccentric: Return each foot to the floor behind you in the plank position, landing softly on the ball of the foot.
steps.rom: Bring the knee as close to the chest as you can without the hips rising; for a slower core-focused version, pause with the knee in.
steps.tempo: Beginners: slow alternating drives, about one per second. Conditioning: fast but controlled for the work interval.
steps.finish: Finish the interval back in a stable high plank with both feet behind you.
steps.exit: Lower your knees to the floor, sit back onto your heels and rest before the next interval.

cues: Drive the knee to the chest

mistakes.m: Hips bouncing up and down or piking high.
mistakes.fix: Slow the pace and keep the hips in line with the shoulders.

mistakes.m: Shoulders drifting behind the hands.
mistakes.fix: Shift forwards so the shoulders sit over the wrists.

mistakes.m: Feet barely moving, so knees never come forwards.
mistakes.fix: Drive each knee fully towards the chest even at a slower pace.

mistakes.m: Lower back sagging as you tire.
mistakes.fix: End the interval early or switch to the slow version.

safety: If your wrists hurt, use fists or push-up handles, or place your hands on a bench.
This raises heart rate quickly; build up interval length gradually, especially if you are new to exercise or have a heart condition.
Stop if you feel low-back pain from the hips sagging.
checks: Make sure the floor or mat is not slippery.
Clear enough space behind you for your legs.
reduceLoad: Slow down or shorten the interval when your hips bounce or sag, your shoulders drift back, your wrists ache or you cannot breathe in rhythm.
regressions: Incline mountain climbers with hands on a bench

programming.rehab: Not a rehabilitation exercise; for gentle core work use the dead bug or bird dog instead.
programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week, often in circuits or finishers.
programming.initialLoad: Start with 20 s intervals at a slow, controlled pace.
programming.judgeLoad: Form should hold for the whole interval; you should be breathing hard but still able to keep the hips level.
programming.progression: Add 5 s per interval each week, then increase speed or reduce rest.
programming.increase: Increase the interval once every round is completed with clean form. It can contribute to calorie burn, but training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the interval the same if your hips start bouncing, and reduce it if your wrists or lower back complain.

name: Pallof press
musclesText: Primary: internal and external obliques, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis. Secondary: gluteus medius and maximus, anterior deltoid, pectoralis major, serratus anterior.

steps.start: Stand side-on to a cable column or band anchor set at chest height, holding the handle with both hands at the centre of your chest.
steps.setup: Set the cable pulley or band anchor at chest height with a single D-handle; step away until there is clear tension on the cable or band at your chest.
steps.feet: Feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, weight even across both feet; a split or half-kneeling stance is a useful variation.
steps.grip: Interlace your fingers around the handle or hold it with both hands stacked, close to your sternum.
steps.posture: Stand tall with ribs stacked over the pelvis, shoulders level and square to the front, not turned towards the anchor.
steps.brace: Brace your trunk and squeeze your glutes so the cable cannot twist you towards the anchor.
steps.initiate: Press the handle straight out from your chest while resisting the pull to rotate.
steps.concentric: Extend your arms fully in front of your sternum, keeping the hands on your midline and the torso square; hold for one to three seconds.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you press out, breathe steadily during the hold, inhale as you bring the hands back.
steps.eccentric: Bring the handle back to your chest slowly, still resisting rotation.
steps.rom: Press to full arm extension and return to the chest; the trunk itself should not move at all.
steps.tempo: 1-2-2-0: one second out, a two-second hold, two seconds back.
steps.finish: Finish each rep with the handle back at the sternum and the body still square.
steps.exit: Walk back towards the anchor to release tension before letting go, then turn round and train the other side.

cues: Do not let it turn you

mistakes.m: Torso rotating towards the anchor.
mistakes.fix: Use less load or step closer to the anchor.

mistakes.m: Hands drifting off the midline.
mistakes.fix: Keep the handle in line with your sternum.

mistakes.m: Leaning away from the cable.
mistakes.fix: Stand tall with your weight even on both feet.

mistakes.m: Rushing the reps.
mistakes.fix: Hold each press for two seconds.

safety: A low-risk option for people with back pain; keep loads modest.
Check bands for nicks or tears before use.
checks: Set the pulley or anchor at chest height.
Check the band anchor or cable clip is secure.
reduceLoad: Reduce the load when you start rotating, leaning or holding your breath.
regressions: Half-kneeling Pallof press with light band

programming.rehab: Commonly used in back rehabilitation to build anti-rotation control with low spinal load; a physiotherapist can help choose load and stance.
programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with a light band or the lightest cable plate.
programming.judgeLoad: There should be no rotation; stop the set when you start twisting.
programming.progression: Add hold time, then reps, then load.
programming.increase: Increase load once you complete all sets with no rotation. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep load if your torso shifts.

name: Cable woodchoppers
musclesText: Primary: internal and external obliques. Secondary: rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis, gluteus maximus and medius, deltoids, thoracic rotators.

steps.start: Stand side-on to a cable column with the pulley at its highest setting, holding the handle with both hands above the shoulder nearest the stack.
steps.setup: Set the pulley at the top position with a single D-handle or rope; select a light weight.
steps.feet: Stand in a wide athletic stance, knees slightly bent, weight on both feet.
steps.grip: Hold the handle with both hands, one over the other, arms nearly straight.
steps.posture: Chest up, spine neutral, shoulders turned towards the high pulley.
steps.brace: Brace your abs and keep the spine long.
steps.initiate: Begin by rotating your hips and trunk away from the stack, pulling the handle down diagonally.
steps.concentric: Pull the handle down and across your body to the outside of the opposite knee, pivoting the back foot.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you chop down, inhale as you return.
steps.eccentric: Return the handle slowly along the same path to the start.
steps.rom: Move from above the shoulder to beside the opposite knee.
steps.tempo: 1-0-2-0: one second chop, two seconds back.
steps.finish: Finish with hips and chest facing the opposite side.
steps.exit: Return to the start, let the weight down, then switch sides.

mistakes.m: Pulling with the arms only while the trunk stays still.
mistakes.fix: Lead with the hips and trunk; the arms just guide the handle.

mistakes.m: Twisting from the lower back with the feet planted.
mistakes.fix: Pivot the back foot so the hips turn with the shoulders.

mistakes.m: Rounding the back at the bottom.
mistakes.fix: Keep the chest up and finish at knee height.

mistakes.m: Load too heavy, yanking the stack.
mistakes.fix: Lighten until the chop and the return are smooth.

safety: Rotate through the hips and upper back, not just the lower back, and pivot the back foot.
Start light if you have back pain; the Pallof press is a lower-risk option.
Keep the return slow so the stack does not pull you off balance.
checks: Check the handle is clipped securely and the pin is fully in.
Clear space on both sides of the column.
reduceLoad: Reduce the weight when the arms take over, the return is uncontrolled, you lose balance or feel pain in the lower back.

programming.rehab: A light half-kneeling chop can feature in later-stage rehab; follow a physiotherapist's guidance.
programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with a light weight you can move smoothly for 15 reps per side.
programming.judgeLoad: Every rep should be smooth with the hips and trunk turning together and a controlled return.
programming.progression: Double progression: add reps per side, then add one plate.
programming.increase: Increase the load when all reps on both sides are smooth at the top of the range. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the load the same if the arms start pulling, and reduce it if the lower back complains.

name: Russian twists
musclesText: Primary: internal and external obliques. Secondary: rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis, iliopsoas.

steps.start: Sit on a mat with knees bent, heels on the floor, and lean back to about 45 degrees holding a plate or medicine ball at your chest.
steps.setup: Choose a light plate (2.5-5 kg) or medicine ball; place a mat under your seat for comfort.
steps.feet: Feet flat with heels down for the easier version, or lift the feet off the floor for the harder one; keep knees together.
steps.grip: Hold the plate by its edges or the ball with both hands, elbows bent, close to your chest.
steps.posture: Lean back with a long spine and chest up; avoid slumping into a rounded lower back.
steps.brace: Brace your abs to hold the lean-back position steady.
steps.initiate: Rotate your ribcage to one side, taking the weight with you.
steps.concentric: Turn your shoulders and the weight towards one hip, then rotate through the centre to the other side, keeping the hips facing forwards.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you rotate to each side, inhale through the centre.
steps.eccentric: Return through the centre under control rather than swinging the weight.
steps.rom: Rotate until the weight is beside the hip; the shoulders turn while the knees stay still.
steps.tempo: Controlled: about one second to each side.
steps.finish: Each side counts as one rep; finish facing forwards.
steps.exit: Bring the weight to your chest, sit upright and place it on the floor beside you.

cues: Turn the ribs, not just the arms

mistakes.m: Swinging the arms while the trunk stays still.
mistakes.fix: Turn your shoulders and keep the weight close to your chest.

mistakes.m: Slumping into a rounded lower back.
mistakes.fix: Lean back less and lengthen through the spine.

mistakes.m: Knees swaying side to side.
mistakes.fix: Keep the knees together and pointing up.

mistakes.m: Moving too fast with a heavy weight.
mistakes.fix: Use a lighter load and a controlled tempo.

safety: Avoid if loaded rotation in flexion aggravates a back condition; the Pallof press is a safer choice.
Keep feet down until you can control the lean-back position.
checks: Use a mat for your tailbone.
Make sure the plate or ball is easy to grip and not too heavy.
reduceLoad: Reduce the weight or put your feet down when you slump, swing or feel pain in the lower back.
regressions: Bodyweight Russian twist with feet down

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with bodyweight or a 2.5 kg plate with the feet down.
programming.judgeLoad: You should finish with steady posture and control.
programming.progression: Add reps, then lift the feet, then add load.
programming.increase: Increase once 15 controlled reps per side are easy. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the load the same if you slump or swing.

name: Hollow-body hold
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis. Secondary: iliopsoas, obliques, rectus femoris.

steps.start: Lie on your back on a mat with legs straight and together and arms by your sides.
steps.setup: Only a mat is needed; a firm surface helps you feel your lower back pressing down.
steps.feet: Legs straight and together with toes pointed; bend the knees into a tuck if the straight-leg version makes your back lift.
steps.grip: Reach your arms overhead beside your ears for the full version, or point them towards your feet for an easier lever.
steps.posture: Lift your shoulder blades and legs a few centimetres off the floor so your body forms a shallow banana shape, lower back pressed into the mat.
steps.brace: Exhale fully, pull your ribs down towards your pelvis and tighten the abs so no gap opens under your lower back.
steps.initiate: Press your lower back down first, then lift your head, arms and legs together.
steps.concentric: Not applicable: isometric hold. Instead, keep reaching long through the fingertips and toes while the lower back stays pressed into the mat.
steps.breathing: Take short, controlled breaths behind the brace; do not hold your breath.
steps.eccentric: Not applicable: isometric hold. Finish by lowering your arms, head and legs to the mat together.
steps.rom: Lower the legs only as far as the lower back stays down; higher legs and arms by your sides make it easier.
steps.tempo: Steady isometric hold, 15-45 s.
steps.finish: Lower your arms and legs slowly to the mat and relax.
steps.exit: Bend your knees, roll onto your side and sit up.

cues: Legs higher if the back lifts

mistakes.m: Lower back arching off the floor.
mistakes.fix: Raise the legs higher, bend the knees or bring the arms down by your sides.

mistakes.m: Straining through the neck.
mistakes.fix: Tuck the chin slightly and keep the gaze on your toes.

mistakes.m: Holding the breath.
mistakes.fix: Take short breaths while keeping the ribs down.

mistakes.m: Lifting the legs so high the hold becomes easy.
mistakes.fix: Lower them gradually as control improves.

safety: Stop if you feel pain in the lower back; it usually means the back has lifted.
If the hip flexors cramp or pinch, use the tuck version and build up gradually.
People with neck problems can rest the head on the mat.
checks: Use a mat on a flat floor.
Clear space for your arms overhead.
reduceLoad: Move to the tuck or arms-down version when your lower back lifts, your neck strains or the hold shakes so much you lose shape.

programming.rehab: The tucked version can be used later in core rehabilitation if a physiotherapist approves.
programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with the tuck hold for 15-20 s.
programming.judgeLoad: The lower back must stay pressed down for the whole hold.
programming.progression: Add time to 30 s, then lengthen the levers (arms overhead, legs straighter and lower).
programming.increase: Lengthen the levers once you hold 30-45 s with the back flat. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the variation the same while the back still lifts near the end.

name: Lying leg raise
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis (lower portion), iliopsoas. Secondary: obliques, rectus femoris, transversus abdominis.

steps.start: Lie on your back on a mat or flat bench with legs straight and together, hands under your hips or gripping the bench behind your head.
steps.setup: On the floor use a mat; on a flat bench lie with your hips near the end and grip the bench sides or the upright behind your head.
steps.feet: Legs together and straight, or knees slightly soft if your hamstrings are tight.
steps.grip: Palms flat under your glutes on the floor, or hands gripping the bench edge behind your head for stability.
steps.posture: Press your lower back gently into the mat or bench and keep your head down.
steps.brace: Exhale and pull your ribs down to set the lower back before lifting.
steps.initiate: Lift your legs together from the hips while keeping the lower back down.
steps.concentric: Raise your legs until they are vertical, then curl the pelvis slightly off the floor or bench to finish with the abs.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you lift, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Lower your legs slowly, stopping when your lower back starts to lift, often a few centimetres above the floor.
steps.rom: Lift to vertical and lower only as far as you can keep the lower back down; on a bench you can lower further only with full control.
steps.tempo: 1-1-3-0: one second up, short pause, three seconds down.
steps.finish: Finish with legs hovering just above the floor or bench, then start the next rep.
steps.exit: Lower your legs to the floor, bend your knees and roll to the side to get up.

cues: Lift from the hips, curl at the top

mistakes.m: Lower back arching as the legs go down.
mistakes.fix: Shorten the range or bend the knees.

mistakes.m: Dropping the legs quickly.
mistakes.fix: Count three seconds on the way down.

mistakes.m: Swinging the legs up with momentum.
mistakes.fix: Pause briefly at the bottom of each rep.

mistakes.m: Pushing hard with the hands.
mistakes.fix: Use the hands only for balance.

safety: Stop if you feel low-back pain; the long lever pulls on the lumbar spine if the brace fails.
On a bench, hold firmly so you do not slide.
checks: Mat or stable bench.
Clear space for your legs.
reduceLoad: Reduce the range or bend the knees when your lower back lifts or aches.

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with bent-knee raises if straight legs make your back arch.
programming.judgeLoad: Each rep should be controlled with the back flat.
programming.progression: Add reps, then slow the lowering, then add ankle weights or move to the hanging version.
programming.increase: Increase difficulty once 15 controlled reps are easy. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep it the same if your lower back lifts.

name: Weighted decline crunch
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis. Secondary: internal and external obliques.

steps.start: Lie back on a decline bench with your feet hooked under the rollers, knees bent, and a weight plate held flat against your chest.
steps.setup: Set the decline to a moderate angle of about 15-30 degrees and lock the foot rollers. Pick up a light plate (2.5-5 kg) before lying back.
steps.feet: Hook both ankles securely under the rollers with knees bent; the feet anchor you but you should not pull hard with the hip flexors.
steps.grip: Hold the plate flat against your upper chest with both arms crossed over it; keep it there throughout.
steps.posture: Start lying back on the pad with a neutral spine and the chin slightly tucked, as if holding an orange under it.
steps.brace: Exhale, pull your ribs down and tighten your abs before you lift.
steps.initiate: Curl your head and shoulders off the bench, leading with the ribcage.
steps.concentric: Crunch up until your shoulder blades are clear of the bench while your lower back stays in contact; this is a crunch, not a full sit-up.
steps.breathing: Exhale as you crunch, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Uncurl slowly back down until your shoulder blades touch the pad.
steps.rom: Short range: from shoulders on the pad to shoulder blades lifted; the lower back never leaves the bench.
steps.tempo: 1-1-2-0: one second up, one-second squeeze, two seconds down.
steps.finish: Return until the shoulder blades touch the pad, keeping tension on the abs.
steps.exit: Sit up with the plate held close, set it down beside the bench, then unhook your feet and step off.

cues: Shoulder blades up, lower back down

mistakes.m: Turning it into a full sit-up with the hip flexors.
mistakes.fix: Stop as soon as the shoulder blades clear the bench.

mistakes.m: Pushing the plate forwards to help.
mistakes.fix: Keep the plate pinned to the chest.

mistakes.m: Jerking the head forwards.
mistakes.fix: Lead with the ribcage and keep the chin tucked.

mistakes.m: Plate too heavy so reps get short and jerky.
mistakes.fix: Drop to a lighter plate.

safety: Avoid if loaded spinal flexion aggravates a back condition.
Hold the plate securely; do not let it slide towards your face.
Sit up before getting off the decline to avoid a head rush.
checks: Check the decline pin and foot rollers are locked.
Have the plate within reach before lying back.
reduceLoad: Reduce the plate when you start jerking, pushing the plate, or lifting the lower back off the bench.

programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with a 2.5-5 kg plate and a moderate angle.
programming.judgeLoad: The last reps should be hard but still a smooth curl with the lower back on the bench.
programming.progression: Double progression: build to the top of the rep range, then add 2.5 kg or steepen the bench.
programming.increase: Add load when all sets reach the top of the rep range with control. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the load if form slips, and reduce it if your back aches.

name: Suitcase carry
musclesText: Primary: internal and external obliques, quadratus lumborum, forearm flexors (grip). Secondary: rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis, upper trapezius, gluteus medius, erector spinae, quadriceps.

steps.start: Stand beside a heavy dumbbell or kettlebell with feet hip-width apart, ready to pick it up with one hand.
steps.setup: Choose a dumbbell or kettlebell that is heavy for one hand and mark out a clear, flat walking lane of 15-30 m, or plan a timed walk.
steps.feet: Feet hip-width apart for the pick-up; walk with normal, slightly shorter steps, placing each foot straight ahead.
steps.grip: Grip the handle in the centre with a full, tight grip, arm straight by your side and the weight just off your thigh.
steps.posture: Stand tall with the shoulders level, ribs over the pelvis and head neutral; do not lean away from or towards the weight.
steps.brace: Brace your trunk, especially the side opposite the weight, which works hardest to stop you tipping sideways.
steps.initiate: Hinge at the hips with a neutral spine to pick up the weight, stand up tall, then take your first controlled step.
steps.concentric: Walk steadily for the set distance or time, keeping the shoulders level and the weight from swinging into your leg.
steps.breathing: Breathe in short, controlled breaths behind the brace; do not hold your breath for the whole walk.
steps.eccentric: Not applicable as a lowering phase: the return is walking back, or turning carefully at the end of the lane with small steps while keeping the torso upright.
steps.rom: Walk the full distance or time only while posture stays tall and shoulders stay level.
steps.tempo: Steady walking pace, about one step per second, smooth and controlled.
steps.finish: Stop with both feet together, still standing tall, at the end of the distance or time.
steps.exit: Hinge at the hips with a neutral spine to place the weight down, then switch hands and repeat on the other side.

mistakes.m: Leaning away from the weight.
mistakes.fix: Use a lighter weight and focus on level shoulders.

mistakes.m: Shoulder on the loaded side dragged down.
mistakes.fix: Pull the shoulder up slightly to level it.

mistakes.m: Rushing and letting the weight swing.
mistakes.fix: Slow the pace and hold the weight still.

mistakes.m: Picking up the weight with a rounded back.
mistakes.fix: Hinge with a flat back and push through the legs.

safety: Pick up and put down the weight with a hip hinge and neutral spine.
Stop if grip fails; do not let the weight drop onto your feet.
Wear supportive shoes and use a clear, flat path.
checks: Check the walking lane is clear and dry.
Check the dumbbell collars or kettlebell handle are secure.
reduceLoad: Reduce the weight when you lean sideways, your shoulders drop unevenly or your grip fails before the distance.

programming.rehab: Light suitcase carries are commonly used in later back rehabilitation to build lateral trunk endurance; ask a physiotherapist about loads.
programming.frequency: 2-3 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with a weight about one-third of your bodyweight in one hand if you are experienced, or lighter if you are new.
programming.judgeLoad: Finish each walk with posture still tall and grip still firm.
programming.progression: Add distance first, then load in 2 kg steps.
programming.increase: Increase when you complete the distance on both sides with level shoulders. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep the load the same if one side is weaker, and reduce if your back aches.

name: V-up
musclesText: Primary: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas. Secondary: obliques, rectus femoris, transversus abdominis.

steps.start: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs straight and arms extended overhead on the floor.
steps.setup: Only a mat is needed; make sure you have room for your arms overhead.
steps.feet: Legs straight and together, toes pointed.
steps.grip: Arms straight overhead, hands together or shoulder-width.
steps.posture: Lie flat with the lower back gently pressed down and ribs drawn in.
steps.brace: Exhale and brace hard before lifting.
steps.initiate: Lift your arms, head and legs together in one movement.
steps.concentric: Bring your arms and legs up so your hands meet your shins or toes over your hips, balancing briefly on your sitting bones.
steps.breathing: Exhale sharply as you rise, inhale as you lower.
steps.eccentric: Lower your arms and legs under control back to the start, keeping the back from slamming down.
steps.rom: Full range from lying flat to the V; bend the knees slightly if needed.
steps.tempo: 1-0-2-0: one second up, two seconds down.
steps.finish: Meet in the V over the hips, then lower.
steps.exit: Lower to the floor, rest, then roll to your side to get up.

cues: Arms and legs meet over the hips

mistakes.m: Lifting the legs much later than the torso.
mistakes.fix: Move both ends at the same time.

mistakes.m: Slamming back down.
mistakes.fix: Lower for two seconds.

mistakes.m: Bending the knees a lot.
mistakes.fix: Bend slightly or use the tuck-up regression.

safety: Avoid if repeated spinal flexion aggravates your lower back.
Build up from the tuck-up and hollow hold; do not force the full range.
Do not slam back down, which jars the back and head.
checks: Use a mat on a flat floor.
Clear space overhead and in front of you.
reduceLoad: Regress to tuck-ups when you cannot keep the legs straight, the arms and legs no longer meet, or you crash on the way down.

programming.frequency: 2 times per week.
programming.initialLoad: Start with tuck-ups if you cannot do five clean V-ups.
programming.judgeLoad: End each set when the arms and legs no longer meet or the lowering becomes uncontrolled.
programming.progression: Add reps, then pause at the top, then hold a light dumbbell or medicine ball.
programming.increase: Increase difficulty when 12 clean reps are easy. Training your abs strengthens them but does not spot-reduce belly fat; fat loss comes from an overall energy deficit.
programming.maintain: Keep it the same if form slips, and reduce volume if your back aches.

name: Treadmill walking
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system (heart and lungs). Secondary: quadriceps, gluteus maximus and medius, hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus.

steps.start: Stand on the side rails of the treadmill, straddling the belt, with the safety clip attached to your clothing before you press start.
steps.setup: Set the grade to 0-2% (1% roughly mimics outdoor walking) and start the belt at a slow speed, around 3 km/h, before stepping on.
steps.feet: Step onto the moving belt one foot at a time, then walk in the middle of the belt with feet about hip-width apart and toes pointing forward.
steps.grip: Let your arms swing naturally from the shoulders with relaxed hands; touch the handrails only to steady yourself when stepping on or off.
steps.posture: Stand tall with your head level, eyes looking forward rather than down at the console, and ribs stacked over your pelvis.
steps.brace: Keep a light, natural tension in your trunk, just enough to stop you sagging or leaning back; you should still be able to chat.
steps.initiate: Once balanced, raise the speed in small steps of 0.3-0.5 km/h until you reach a brisk pace of roughly 4.5-6.5 km/h.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: land softly on your heel, roll through the foot and push off from the big toe, with the rear leg extending behind you.
steps.breathing: Breathe rhythmically through your nose or mouth; at a brisk pace you should be breathing faster but still able to speak in full sentences.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: let the swing leg travel forward relaxed from the hip, keeping your stride natural rather than overreaching.
steps.rom: Use a natural stride length; if your foot lands well in front of your knee, shorten your step and increase cadence.
steps.tempo: Not applicable as a rep tempo; aim for a steady cadence of roughly 100-120 steps per minute for brisk walking.
steps.finish: Finish with 2-3 minutes of slower walking to let your heart rate settle gradually.
steps.exit: Reduce the speed to a slow walk, press stop, wait for the belt to halt fully, then hold the rail and step off to the side.

cues: Stay in the middle of the belt
Short, quick steps if you overstride

mistakes.m: Holding onto the handrails or console throughout
mistakes.fix: Let go and lower the speed until you can walk unaided; holding on reduces the work and alters your gait.

mistakes.m: Drifting to the back of the belt
mistakes.fix: Stay within arm's length of the console and slightly reduce speed if you keep drifting.

mistakes.m: Looking down at feet or phone
mistakes.fix: Keep your eyes on a point ahead at eye level to maintain posture and balance.

mistakes.m: Overstriding with a heavy heel strike
mistakes.fix: Take shorter, quicker steps so your foot lands closer to beneath your hips.

safety: Always attach the safety clip so the belt stops if you fall back.
Never step onto a belt already moving fast; start slowly and build up.
Stop if you feel chest pain, unusual breathlessness, dizziness or palpitations, and seek medical advice.
checks: Check the emergency stop and safety clip are working before you start.
Confirm the grade is set to 0-2% and the starting speed is low.
Wear supportive, laced trainers and keep the area behind the treadmill clear.
reduceLoad: Slow down or lower the grade if you cannot speak in full sentences when aiming for an easy session, if your gait becomes unsteady, or if you feel joint pain in the knees, hips or feet.
regressions: Outdoor walking at an easy pace
Walking with a light handrail touch for balance

endurance.rir: RPE 3-5 out of 10; able to talk in full sentences

programming.rehab: Short, frequent walks of 5-15 minutes at a comfortable pace suit gentle reconditioning after illness or injury; follow your physiotherapist's guidance on duration and speed.
programming.frequency: 3-7 times per week; walking is low stress and can be done daily
programming.initialLoad: Start with 10-20 minutes at a speed where you can talk comfortably, typically 4-5 km/h on a 0-1% grade.
programming.judgeLoad: Use the talk test: you should be breathing noticeably faster but still able to hold a conversation, roughly RPE 3-5 out of 10.
programming.progression: Add 5 minutes to sessions each week first, then add 0.2-0.3 km/h of speed or 1% grade once you can walk 45-60 minutes.
programming.increase: Increase when the current duration and speed feel easy (RPE below 3) for two or three sessions in a row.
programming.maintain: Keep duration the same or reduce it if you are sore the next day, sleeping poorly, or if joint discomfort appears during the walk.

name: Incline treadmill walking
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system, gluteus maximus. Secondary: hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus, quadriceps, erector spinae (postural).

steps.start: Straddle the belt with the safety clip attached, then start the treadmill at a slow speed on a flat grade.
steps.setup: Walk for 3-5 minutes flat to warm up, then raise the grade in steps to between 5% and 12%, lowering speed to roughly 4-5.5 km/h as the grade rises.
steps.feet: Walk with feet hip-width apart in the middle of the belt, letting your whole foot contact the belt rather than staying on your toes.
steps.grip: Swing your arms freely without holding the rails; holding on and leaning back removes much of the incline's benefit.
steps.posture: Lean very slightly forward from the ankles, not from the waist, keeping your chest up and spine long.
steps.brace: Keep your trunk gently braced so your lower back does not arch as you lean into the hill.
steps.initiate: Once the grade is set, settle into a steady pace you can sustain without touching the handrails.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: drive the belt back by pushing through the whole foot and squeezing the glute of the stance leg as the hip extends.
steps.breathing: Breathe steadily and rhythmically; you should feel your breathing deepen but still be able to say a few sentences.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: bring the swing leg through with a slight lift of the knee to clear the incline, landing with the foot under your body.
steps.rom: Use a full hip extension on each step, letting the back leg straighten behind you before it swings forward.
steps.tempo: Not applicable as a rep tempo; aim for a steady, unhurried step rate rather than rushing short steps.
steps.finish: Lower the grade back to 0-1% for the final 3-5 minutes to cool down.
steps.exit: With the grade flat and speed slowed, press stop, wait for the belt to stop and step off to the side holding the rail.

cues: Lean from the ankles, not the waist

mistakes.m: Holding the rails and leaning back
mistakes.fix: Reduce the grade or speed until you can walk hands-free, then progress the grade gradually.

mistakes.m: Hunching forward at the waist
mistakes.fix: Stand tall and lean slightly from the ankles, keeping your chest up.

mistakes.m: Walking on the toes only
mistakes.fix: Let the heel and whole foot contact the belt to share the load between calves and hips.

mistakes.m: Jumping straight to a steep grade
mistakes.fix: Increase the grade by 1-2% at a time after a flat warm-up.

safety: Attach the safety clip; falls backwards are more likely on a steep incline.
Steep grades load the calves and Achilles tendons heavily; build exposure gradually if you have a history of Achilles or calf problems.
Lower the grade if you feel pain in the lower back, shins or Achilles rather than pushing through.
checks: Check that the incline control works and returns to flat.
Confirm the safety clip is attached and the emergency stop is within reach.
Make sure your laces are tied and the belt area is dry.
reduceLoad: Lower the grade or speed if you need the handrails to keep up, cannot speak a short sentence, notice calf or Achilles tightness building, or your posture collapses into a forward hunch.

endurance.reps: 15-45 min continuous, or 3-5 x 5 min at higher grade with 2 min flat
endurance.rest: 2 min flat walking between hill blocks
endurance.rir: RPE 4-6 out of 10; able to speak in short sentences

programming.frequency: 2-5 times per week; allow a day between steep sessions if your calves feel tight
programming.initialLoad: Start at 5% grade and 4.5 km/h for 15-20 minutes, adjusting so you can walk without holding on.
programming.judgeLoad: Breathing should be deep but controlled, about RPE 4-6, and your calves should not cramp or burn severely.
programming.progression: Increase duration first, then add 1% grade per week up to 12%, keeping speed steady.
programming.increase: Increase when you complete the session hands-free at RPE 4 or less on two consecutive sessions.
programming.maintain: Keep the grade the same if your heart rate is climbing more than usual for the same session, or reduce it if calves, shins or Achilles stay sore the next day.

name: Jogging
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system. Secondary: quadriceps, gluteus maximus and medius, hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus, iliopsoas.

steps.start: Begin with 5 minutes of brisk walking, either outdoors or on a treadmill at 0-1% grade, to raise your heart rate gradually.
steps.setup: Outdoors, choose a flat, even route with good lighting; on a treadmill, set a 1% grade and a starting speed of around 7-9 km/h.
steps.feet: Run with feet landing roughly under your hips, toes pointing forward, and a narrow, natural track rather than crossing over.
steps.grip: Bend your elbows to about 90 degrees and swing the arms forward and back, not across your body, with loose hands.
steps.posture: Run tall with your head over your shoulders and a slight whole-body lean forward from the ankles.
steps.brace: Hold light trunk tension so your pelvis stays level and your torso does not twist excessively with each stride.
steps.initiate: Break from the walk into a slow jog with short, light steps, letting your pace settle over the first few minutes.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: land softly with the foot close to beneath your body and push off by extending the hip, knee and ankle together.
steps.breathing: Breathe in a relaxed rhythm, such as in for two or three steps and out for two or three; you should be able to talk in full sentences.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: let the heel come up towards the hips naturally and swing the knee forward without reaching out with the foot.
steps.rom: Keep strides short and comfortable; a cadence of roughly 160-175 steps per minute reduces overstriding for most people.
steps.tempo: Not applicable as a rep tempo; keep an easy, even pace you could hold for 30 minutes or more.
steps.finish: Ease back to a walk for the final 3-5 minutes to cool down.
steps.exit: Outdoors, finish somewhere safe off the road; on a treadmill, slow to a walk, stop the belt fully and step off to the side.

mistakes.m: Running too fast on easy days
mistakes.fix: Slow down until you pass the talk test; walk breaks are fine.

mistakes.m: Overstriding and landing on the heel far ahead of the body
mistakes.fix: Shorten your stride and take slightly quicker steps.

mistakes.m: Increasing weekly distance too quickly
mistakes.fix: Increase total weekly running time by no more than about 10% per week.

mistakes.m: Tense shoulders and clenched fists
mistakes.fix: Drop your shoulders and keep hands loose, as if holding a crisp without breaking it.

safety: Build up gradually with run-walk intervals if you are new to running, to let bones and tendons adapt.
Stop if you develop localised bone pain in the shin or foot, as this can signal a stress injury.
Outdoors, wear visible clothing, face oncoming traffic where there is no pavement and keep music low enough to hear traffic.
checks: Check that your trainers are in good condition and suited to running.
Plan a route with even surfaces, or set the treadmill safety clip.
Carry water for runs longer than about 45 minutes or in hot weather.
reduceLoad: Slow down or walk if you cannot speak in full sentences, if your form deteriorates into shuffling or heavy landing, or if joint, shin or foot pain appears.

endurance.reps: 20-45 min continuous, or run-walk intervals totalling 20-30 min
endurance.rest: walk breaks of 1-2 min as needed
endurance.rir: RPE 3-5 out of 10; full sentences possible

programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week with at least one rest or cross-training day between runs for beginners
programming.initialLoad: Begin with run-walk intervals such as 1 minute jogging and 2 minutes walking, repeated 6-8 times.
programming.judgeLoad: Use the talk test: you should be able to speak in full sentences, roughly RPE 3-5, with breathing controlled.
programming.progression: Lengthen run intervals and shorten walk breaks until you can jog 20-30 minutes continuously, then add time gradually.
programming.increase: Increase when the current session feels easy and you have no lingering soreness the following day.
programming.maintain: Hold the same volume, or reduce it, if you have niggles in the shins, knees or feet, poor sleep, or if your heart rate at a given pace is unusually high.

name: Running intervals
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system (aerobic and anaerobic capacity). Secondary: quadriceps, gluteus maximus, hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus, iliopsoas.

steps.start: Warm up with 8-10 minutes of easy jogging followed by a few short 15-20 second strides at a quicker pace.
steps.setup: Use a flat track, path or treadmill; on a treadmill, preset your fast and recovery speeds so you change speed rather than jumping on and off the belt.
steps.feet: Run with feet landing under your hips; during hard efforts you will naturally land more on the forefoot and midfoot.
steps.grip: Drive your arms powerfully forward and back with elbows bent at about 90 degrees, keeping hands relaxed.
steps.posture: Stay tall with a slight forward lean from the ankles, increasing the lean a little as you accelerate.
steps.brace: Keep your trunk firm during hard efforts so your pelvis stays level and your power goes into the ground.
steps.initiate: Accelerate smoothly over the first 5-10 seconds of each work interval rather than bursting off instantly.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: run 30-60 seconds hard at RPE 7-9, pushing the ground back forcefully with quick, powerful strides.
steps.breathing: Breathing will be heavy during work intervals; focus on deep exhalations, then let breathing settle during recovery.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: slow to an easy jog or walk for 60-120 seconds, letting your heart rate drop before the next effort.
steps.rom: Keep your stride natural and avoid reaching; speed should come from more force and quicker turnover, not longer reaches.
steps.tempo: Use a work-to-rest ratio of 1:2 to start, for example 30 seconds hard and 60 seconds easy, moving towards 1:1 as fitness improves.
steps.finish: Finish the final interval under control, then jog or walk easily for 5-10 minutes to cool down.
steps.exit: On a treadmill, drop to recovery speed before stopping the belt; never jump off a fast-moving belt onto the side rails.

mistakes.m: Sprinting the first interval and fading badly
mistakes.fix: Choose a pace you can repeat for every interval; the last should be as fast as the first.

mistakes.m: Skipping the warm-up
mistakes.fix: Always jog easily and include a few strides before the first hard effort.

mistakes.m: Doing interval sessions too often
mistakes.fix: Limit hard interval sessions to one or two per week, with easy days between.

mistakes.m: Leaning back or overstriding when tired
mistakes.fix: Stay tall with a slight forward lean and shorten your stride.

safety: Only progress to intervals once you can jog 20-30 minutes comfortably.
Hamstring and calf strains are more likely at high speed, so build speed over weeks and stop if you feel a sudden sharp pull.
Stop immediately if you feel chest pain, faintness or an irregular heartbeat.
checks: On a treadmill, preset speeds and test the speed buttons before starting, with the safety clip attached.
Outdoors, choose a flat, unobstructed stretch away from traffic.
Have water available and use a timer you can read easily.
reduceLoad: Reduce the speed or number of intervals if you cannot hold the target pace, your form breaks down, your heart rate does not recover during the rest period, or you feel any muscle tightness that is worsening.

endurance.rir: RPE 7-9 out of 10 on work intervals; only a few words possible

programming.frequency: 1-2 times per week, with at least 48 hours and easy sessions between hard interval days
programming.initialLoad: Start with 6 x 30 seconds at a pace you could hold for about 3-4 minutes, with 90 seconds of easy recovery.
programming.judgeLoad: Each interval should feel hard (RPE 7-9) yet repeatable; if the last two are much slower than the first, the pace was too fast.
programming.progression: Add one or two intervals, lengthen work periods by 10-15 seconds, or shorten recovery, changing only one variable at a time.
programming.increase: Increase when you complete every interval at the target pace with good form and feel recovered within 24-48 hours.
programming.maintain: Keep the session the same or drop intervals if you feel fatigued from previous training, slept poorly, or notice any lingering calf, hamstring or Achilles discomfort.

name: Stationary cycling
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system, quadriceps (vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, rectus femoris). Secondary: gluteus maximus, hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus.

steps.start: Stand beside the bike and adjust it fully before mounting, then sit on the saddle with both feet secured on the pedals.
steps.setup: Set saddle height so your knee keeps a slight bend of about 25-35 degrees when the pedal is at the bottom; a quick check is that your heel just reaches the pedal with the leg straight. On a spin bike, set the saddle fore-aft so your knee sits roughly over the pedal axle at the 3 o'clock position, and set the handlebars level with or slightly above the saddle.
steps.feet: Place the ball of each foot over the pedal axle, tighten straps or clip in, and keep feet pointing straight ahead with knees tracking over the toes.
steps.grip: Hold the handlebars lightly with relaxed hands and a soft bend in the elbows; avoid gripping hard or locking your arms.
steps.posture: Hinge slightly forward from the hips with a long, neutral spine, keeping your shoulders down and away from your ears.
steps.brace: Keep gentle trunk tension so your hips stay still on the saddle rather than rocking side to side.
steps.initiate: Start pedalling with light resistance and a cadence of 70-90 revolutions per minute for 3-5 minutes to warm up.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: push the pedal down and slightly forward from the 12 to 5 o'clock position, using hips and thighs together.
steps.breathing: Breathe rhythmically and deeply; for steady sessions you should be able to talk in sentences.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: let the pedal travel smoothly through the bottom and back up, lifting gently if your feet are strapped in.
steps.rom: Each leg should move through a full pedal circle without your hips rocking or your knee locking out at the bottom.
steps.tempo: Not applicable as a rep tempo; aim for 70-100 revolutions per minute on steady efforts.
steps.finish: Spend the last 3-5 minutes pedalling with light resistance to cool down.
steps.exit: On a spin bike with a fixed flywheel, slow gradually or press the brake lever before unclipping; then step off carefully.

cues: Slight knee bend at the bottom
Ball of foot over the axle

mistakes.m: Saddle too low, causing excessive knee bend
mistakes.fix: Raise the saddle until there is a slight bend at the bottom of the stroke.

mistakes.m: Saddle too high, making the hips rock
mistakes.fix: Lower the saddle so your hips stay level and your foot does not reach for the pedal.

mistakes.m: Bouncing at high cadence with too little resistance
mistakes.fix: Add resistance until your pedal stroke is smooth and controlled.

mistakes.m: Knees flaring out or caving in
mistakes.fix: Align feet straight on the pedals and keep knees tracking over the second toe.

safety: Incorrect saddle height is a common cause of front-of-knee pain; adjust before every session.
Spin bikes with fixed flywheels keep moving if you stop pedalling, so use the brake to stop rather than lifting feet off.
Stand up out of the saddle only with enough resistance to support your weight.
checks: Check the saddle and handlebar pins are fully locked.
Confirm pedal straps are secure or cleats are clipped in properly.
Test the resistance knob and emergency brake before you start.
reduceLoad: Lower the resistance if your cadence drops below about 60 revolutions per minute on steady work, your hips start rocking, you cannot hold a conversation on easy rides, or you feel knee pain.
progressions: Standing climbs on a spin bike

endurance.reps: 20-60 min steady, or 6-10 x 30-60 s hard intervals

programming.rehab: Low-resistance cycling for 10-20 minutes is a common, joint-friendly option for knee and hip rehabilitation; follow your physiotherapist's guidance on saddle height and duration.
programming.frequency: 3-6 times per week; easy sessions can be done on consecutive days
programming.initialLoad: Begin with 15-20 minutes at a resistance where you can pedal at 80 revolutions per minute and still talk comfortably.
programming.judgeLoad: On steady rides, use the talk test and RPE 3-5; on intervals, the effort should feel hard but repeatable for every interval.
programming.progression: Add 5 minutes per week to steady rides, then increase resistance or watts by about 5-10%; for intervals, add one interval or shorten recovery.
programming.increase: Increase when you can complete the session at the target effort with a steady cadence and no next-day joint pain.
programming.maintain: Keep the session the same if your heart rate is higher than usual for the same output, or reduce it if knee or hip discomfort develops.

name: Outdoor cycling
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system, quadriceps. Secondary: gluteus maximus, hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus, trunk stabilisers.

steps.start: Stand over the bike's top tube with brakes applied, helmet fastened and lights on, before you push off from a safe, quiet spot.
steps.setup: Set the saddle so your knee has a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke, check tyre pressure matches the range printed on the tyre wall, and check both brakes stop the wheels firmly.
steps.feet: Place the balls of your feet over the pedal axles, or clip in if you use cleats, keeping feet straight and knees tracking over the toes.
steps.grip: Hold the bars with relaxed hands, fingers ready to cover the brake levers, and keep a slight bend in your elbows to absorb bumps.
steps.posture: Lean forward from the hips with a long back and relaxed shoulders, keeping your head up so you can scan the road ahead.
steps.brace: Hold light trunk tension to keep the bike stable and your hips quiet on the saddle.
steps.initiate: Push off in an easy gear, pedalling gently for the first 5-10 minutes to warm up before increasing effort.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: drive the pedal down from the top of the stroke, shifting to an easier gear on climbs to keep cadence around 70-90 revolutions per minute.
steps.breathing: Breathe steadily; on easy rides you should be able to talk, while hills will raise your breathing for short periods.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: let the pedal circle smoothly back up and freewheel or ease off on descents, staying alert and covering the brakes.
steps.rom: Use a full, smooth pedal circle; shift gears early rather than grinding at very low cadence.
steps.tempo: Not applicable as a rep tempo; keep a steady cadence and change gears to match the terrain.
steps.finish: Ease off for the final 5-10 minutes in a light gear to cool down.
steps.exit: Brake to a full stop, unclip or put a foot down on the kerb side, then dismount away from traffic.

cues: Look ahead, not at your wheel

mistakes.m: Riding in too hard a gear
mistakes.fix: Shift down to keep cadence above about 70 revolutions per minute, especially on hills.

mistakes.m: Riding in the gutter or too close to parked cars
mistakes.fix: Ride a safe distance from the kerb and at least a door's width from parked cars.

mistakes.m: Gripping the bars with locked arms
mistakes.fix: Bend your elbows and relax your grip so the bike can move beneath you.

mistakes.m: Skipping pre-ride checks
mistakes.fix: Check brakes, tyres and lights before every ride.

safety: Always wear a properly fitted helmet and use front and rear lights plus bright or reflective clothing for visibility.
Follow the Highway Code, signal clearly and stay alert; avoid headphones that block traffic noise.
Take extra care on wet roads, painted lines and metal covers, braking earlier and cornering more gently.
checks: Check both brakes engage firmly and tyres are inflated within the printed range.
Make sure lights are charged and the helmet buckle is fastened snugly.
Carry a phone, water, and a basic puncture repair kit or spare tube.
reduceLoad: Ease off or choose flatter routes if you cannot hold a conversation on easy rides, your pedalling becomes ragged, you feel light-headed, or you develop knee, hip or lower back pain.
regressions: Short flat rides on traffic-free paths

endurance.reps: 30-120 min steady, or 4-8 x 2-4 min hill efforts
endurance.rest: easy riding for 2-4 min between hill efforts

programming.frequency: 2-5 times per week; longer rides once a week with shorter easy rides in between
programming.initialLoad: Start with 30-45 minute rides on flat, quiet routes at a conversational effort.
programming.judgeLoad: Use the talk test on steady rides; on climbs, breathing should be hard but recover within a minute or two on the flat.
programming.progression: Increase ride duration by about 10-15% per week, then add hillier routes or intervals.
programming.increase: Increase when rides at the current distance feel comfortable and you recover fully by the next day.
programming.maintain: Keep distance the same in poor weather, after a hard week, or if saddle, knee or back discomfort appears; get a bike fit if discomfort persists.

name: Rowing machine
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system, rhomboids and middle trapezius, quadriceps. Secondary: gluteus maximus, hamstrings, latissimus dorsi, biceps brachii, erector spinae, forearm flexors.

steps.start: Sit on the seat at the catch position: shins near vertical, arms straight reaching for the handle, and torso leaning slightly forward from the hips.
steps.setup: Set the damper on an air rower to about 3-5 (or a moderate level on a magnetic rower); higher settings feel heavier but do not necessarily mean a better workout.
steps.feet: Strap your feet in so the strap crosses the widest part of your foot, with the heels resting in the foot cups.
steps.grip: Hold the handle with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder-width apart, fingers hooked and wrists flat.
steps.posture: Keep a long, neutral spine with your chest proud, leaning forward slightly from the hips at the catch rather than rounding.
steps.brace: Brace your trunk before each drive so the force from your legs transfers through your body to the handle.
steps.initiate: Begin the drive by pushing your feet into the footplate while your arms stay straight.
steps.concentric: Effort phase (drive): push with the legs first, then swing the torso back to about 11 o'clock, then pull the handle to your lower ribs with elbows close to the body; this is the finish position.
steps.breathing: Exhale during the drive and inhale during the recovery; at higher stroke rates you may take two breaths per stroke.
steps.eccentric: Recovery: reverse the order, extending the arms first, then hinging the torso forward from the hips, then bending the knees to slide back to the catch.
steps.rom: Row from a compressed catch to a full leg extension; do not slide so far forward that your shins pass vertical or your back rounds.
steps.tempo: Recovery should take about twice as long as the drive; use 18-24 strokes per minute for steady rowing and 26-32 for hard intervals.
steps.finish: Finish each stroke with legs straight, torso slightly back and the handle at your lower ribs before beginning the recovery.
steps.exit: Stop at the catch, rest the handle in its holder, release the foot straps and stand up carefully.
