mistakes.m: Pulling with the arms before the legs have finished pushing
mistakes.fix: Keep arms straight until the legs are nearly extended, then swing back and pull.

mistakes.m: Rounding the back at the catch
mistakes.fix: Slide forward only as far as you can keep a long spine, hinging from the hips.

mistakes.m: Rushing the recovery
mistakes.fix: Count roughly one on the drive and two on the recovery.

mistakes.m: Damper set to the maximum
mistakes.fix: Lower the damper to 3-5 so the stroke feels like a fast boat rather than dragging an anchor.

mistakes.m: Knees bending before the handle passes them on the recovery
mistakes.fix: Extend arms and pivot the torso forward first so the handle clears the knees.

safety: Keep a neutral spine at the catch; repeated rounding under load can aggravate the lower back.
Build volume gradually as rowing places sustained demand on the lower back and hands.
Stop if you develop sharp back pain or tingling down the leg.
checks: Check the foot straps are tight across the widest part of each foot.
Set the damper or resistance level and reset the monitor.
Make sure the rail is clean and nothing is behind the seat track.
reduceLoad: Lower the stroke rate or intensity if your sequencing breaks down, your back begins to round at the catch, you cannot hold your target split, or lower back discomfort appears.
regressions: Steady rowing at low stroke rate
progressions: Rowing intervals such as 8 x 250 m

endurance.reps: 20-40 min steady, or 250-500 m hard intervals
endurance.rir: RPE 3-5 steady at 18-22 strokes per minute; RPE 7-9 on intervals

programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week
programming.initialLoad: Begin with 10-15 minutes at 18-22 strokes per minute at a pace you can sustain while focused on technique.
programming.judgeLoad: Use the split time (time per 500 m) and talk test; a steady split should be repeatable for the whole session without form breakdown.
programming.progression: Add 5 minutes to steady sessions weekly, then improve your average 500 m split by a few seconds, or add intervals.
programming.increase: Increase when your stroke sequence stays clean throughout and you complete the session at the target split.
programming.maintain: Keep the session the same if your technique deteriorates late in the session or your lower back feels tight afterwards.

name: Elliptical
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system. Secondary: quadriceps, gluteus maximus, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, pectoralis major and upper back (when using moving handles).

steps.start: Hold the static handles, step onto the pedals one foot at a time, and stand tall before you start moving.
steps.setup: Set a low resistance level and, if adjustable, a moderate incline or stride length that feels natural for your height.
steps.feet: Place your whole foot in the centre of each pedal, toes pointing forward and heels down, without gripping with your toes.
steps.grip: Hold the moving handles lightly at about chest height, pushing and pulling in rhythm with your legs, or use the static handles for balance.
steps.posture: Stand upright with your weight over your feet, shoulders relaxed and head level, rather than leaning on the handles.
steps.brace: Keep a light brace through your trunk so your hips stay level and do not sway.
steps.initiate: Begin striding forward slowly; the console will usually wake up as you start moving.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: press down and back through the heel and midfoot, extending the hip and knee while the opposite arm pushes forward.
steps.breathing: Breathe rhythmically; on steady sessions you should be able to talk in sentences.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: let the pedal rise and travel forward smoothly while you pull the handle back with the same-side arm.
steps.rom: Use the full elliptical path the machine provides; keep the knee soft, never snapping into lockout.
steps.tempo: Not applicable as a rep tempo; aim for about 120-160 strides per minute, adjusting resistance rather than spinning fast.
steps.finish: Lower the resistance for the final 3-5 minutes to cool down.
steps.exit: Slow to a stop, let the pedals come to rest with one at its lowest point, hold the static handles and step down.

mistakes.m: Leaning heavily on the handles
mistakes.fix: Use the handles lightly and keep your weight over your feet.

mistakes.m: Rising onto the toes
mistakes.fix: Keep your heels in contact with the pedals to reduce calf and foot strain.

mistakes.m: Very low resistance with fast, bouncy strides
mistakes.fix: Add resistance until each stride feels smooth and purposeful.

mistakes.m: Hunching over the console
mistakes.fix: Stand upright with your chest up and eyes forward.

safety: The pedals continue moving with momentum, so slow down fully before stepping off.
Numb toes are common when pressing through the forefoot; shift pressure to the heel and loosen laces if it happens.
Stop if you feel knee or hip pain rather than pushing through.
checks: Check pedals and handles are secure and the machine sits level on the floor.
Set resistance low for the warm-up.
Wear supportive trainers with tied laces.
reduceLoad: Reduce the resistance if you cannot keep a smooth stride rate, you must lean on the handles, you cannot talk on an easy session, or joint discomfort appears.

endurance.reps: 20-45 min steady, or 30-60 s hard intervals

programming.rehab: Because there is no impact, short steady sessions of 10-20 minutes at low resistance suit people returning from lower-limb injuries; check with your physiotherapist first.
programming.frequency: 3-6 times per week
programming.initialLoad: Begin with 15-20 minutes at a low resistance that allows you to talk easily while striding smoothly.
programming.judgeLoad: Use the talk test and RPE; steady sessions should be RPE 3-5, intervals hard but repeatable.
programming.progression: Add 5 minutes per week, then increase resistance by one level or add short intervals.
programming.increase: Increase when the session feels easy (RPE below 3) for two sessions in a row.
programming.maintain: Keep resistance the same or reduce it if you feel joint discomfort, unusual fatigue, or numbness in the feet.

name: Stair climber
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system, gluteus maximus, quadriceps. Secondary: hamstrings, gastrocnemius and soleus.

steps.start: Stand on the bottom step with both feet, holding the side rails lightly, before you press start.
steps.setup: Select a slow starting speed, typically level 3-5 or around 30-50 steps per minute, so you can settle into the rhythm.
steps.feet: Place your whole foot on each step, not just the toes, with feet hip-width apart and knees tracking over the toes.
steps.grip: Rest your fingertips on the rails only for balance, or let your arms swing naturally; avoid hanging your weight on the rails.
steps.posture: Stand tall with a slight forward lean from the hips, keeping your chest up and head level.
steps.brace: Keep your trunk lightly braced so you do not slump forward or let the hips drop as you tire.
steps.initiate: Begin stepping as the stairs start to move, matching your pace to the machine before increasing speed.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: drive through the whole foot of the leading leg, straightening the hip and knee to lift your body onto the step.
steps.breathing: Breathe steadily; the effort rises quickly, so slow the machine if you cannot speak in short sentences.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: lift the trailing leg to the next step in a controlled way, without stomping.
steps.rom: Use one full step at a time; skipping steps is an advanced variation for short periods only.
steps.tempo: Not applicable as a rep tempo; keep a smooth, constant rhythm that matches the machine speed.
steps.finish: Reduce the speed for the last 2-3 minutes to cool down.
steps.exit: Lower the speed to the minimum, press stop, wait for the stairs to halt fully, then step off holding the rails.

cues: Slow it down rather than hang on

mistakes.m: Leaning on the rails with locked arms
mistakes.fix: Lower the speed until you can climb with just a fingertip touch.

mistakes.m: Stepping on the toes only
mistakes.fix: Place the whole foot on each step and push through the heel.

mistakes.m: Hunched posture
mistakes.fix: Keep your chest up with only a slight forward lean.

mistakes.m: Speed set too high from the start
mistakes.fix: Start slow, then increase by one level at a time after warming up.

safety: The stairs keep moving, so never look away for long or let go suddenly; use the emergency stop if you lose your footing.
Build up gradually if you have knee or hip issues, as each step loads the joint through a large range.
Stop and lower the speed if you feel dizzy or unsteady.
checks: Locate the emergency stop and check it works.
Make sure laces are tied and nothing hangs loose near the steps.
Start the machine at its slowest setting.
reduceLoad: Lower the speed if you need to hang on the rails, cannot speak in short sentences, your feet start missing steps, or you feel knee pain.

endurance.reps: 10-30 min steady, or 1-2 min faster intervals
endurance.rest: 1-2 min at slow speed between intervals

programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week
programming.initialLoad: Start with 8-10 minutes at a slow speed where you can climb without holding the rails.
programming.judgeLoad: Breathing should be deep but controlled; use RPE 4-6 and the ability to speak short sentences as a guide.
programming.progression: Add 2-3 minutes per week, then raise speed by one level or include intervals.
programming.increase: Increase when you can finish the session hands-free at RPE 5 or less.
programming.maintain: Keep the session the same if your legs feel heavy from lower-body training or if knee discomfort appears.

name: Skipping rope
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system, gastrocnemius and soleus. Secondary: quadriceps, forearm flexors and extensors, anterior deltoid, trunk stabilisers.

steps.start: Stand tall with the rope behind your heels, holding a handle in each hand at hip height.
steps.setup: Size the rope by standing on its middle with one foot; the handles should reach roughly to your armpits for a beginner. Use a flat, slightly forgiving surface such as a gym floor or mat.
steps.feet: Keep feet together or hip-width apart, weight on the balls of the feet, knees softly bent.
steps.grip: Hold the handles lightly with elbows close to your sides and hands slightly in front of your hips, turning the rope with your wrists rather than your arms.
steps.posture: Stand upright with your head level and eyes forward, shoulders relaxed.
steps.brace: Hold a light brace through your trunk so your body moves as one unit with each bounce.
steps.initiate: Swing the rope over your head with a flick of the wrists and jump just as it approaches your feet.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: spring 2-3 cm off the floor from the balls of your feet, using the ankles and calves like springs.
steps.breathing: Breathe rhythmically through each set; do not hold your breath as you concentrate.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: land softly on the balls of your feet with knees slightly bent, letting the heels kiss the floor without slamming down.
steps.rom: Jump only high enough to clear the rope; big jumps waste energy and increase impact.
steps.tempo: Aim for a steady rhythm of about 100-140 turns per minute with one jump per turn.
steps.finish: Stop the rope with a controlled step-through or let it catch against your feet at the end of the interval.
steps.exit: Let the rope come to rest, step out of it and lay it flat away from walkways.

cues: Light on the balls of the feet

mistakes.m: Jumping too high
mistakes.fix: Jump just 2-3 cm off the floor, only enough to clear the rope.

mistakes.m: Turning the rope with the whole arm
mistakes.fix: Keep elbows close and turn from the wrists.

mistakes.m: Double bouncing between turns without control
mistakes.fix: Practise a steady single bounce, slowing the rope down if needed.

mistakes.m: Landing flat-footed and stiff-legged
mistakes.fix: Land on the balls of the feet with soft knees.

safety: Skipping is high-impact for the calves and Achilles; build volume over weeks and avoid concrete where possible.
Stop if you develop shin pain or pain at the back of the heel, as these can signal overuse.
Check the ceiling height and space around you to avoid catching the rope on people or objects.
checks: Check the rope length and that the handles spin freely.
Clear a space of at least 2 metres around you.
Wear cushioned, supportive trainers.
reduceLoad: Reduce the duration or take more rest if your rhythm breaks down repeatedly, landings become heavy, or your calves or shins become sore.

programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week, avoiding consecutive days while you build tolerance
programming.initialLoad: Start with 6-8 rounds of 20-30 seconds skipping and 40-60 seconds rest.
programming.judgeLoad: You should be able to skip with a consistent rhythm and few trips throughout each round; if you trip constantly, slow the rope.
programming.progression: Add 10 seconds per round or one extra round each week, then reduce rest.
programming.increase: Increase when you complete all rounds with steady rhythm and no calf or shin soreness the next day.
programming.maintain: Keep the volume the same if your calves or Achilles feel stiff the next morning, or reduce it if shin pain develops.

name: Sled pushes
musclesText: Primary: quadriceps, gluteus maximus, cardiovascular system. Secondary: gastrocnemius and soleus, hamstrings, triceps brachii, pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, trunk stabilisers.

steps.start: Stand behind the loaded sled on turf, hands on the vertical or low handles, leaning forward with one foot slightly behind you.
steps.setup: Load the sled with plates appropriate to the surface; turf grip varies, so test the load with a short push. Use the high handles for an upright push and the low handles for a more forward lean.
steps.feet: Stagger your feet hip-width apart, with the rear foot ready to drive and weight on the balls of the feet.
steps.grip: Grip the handles with straight or slightly bent arms, locking the elbows enough to transfer force without collapsing.
steps.posture: Lean forward so your body forms a straight line from head to rear heel at about 45 degrees, keeping your back flat.
steps.brace: Brace your trunk hard, as for a heavy lift, so force travels from your legs into the sled.
steps.initiate: Drive the first step powerfully through the front foot to overcome the sled's starting friction.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: take short, powerful steps, pushing each foot back into the turf and fully extending the hip and knee.
steps.breathing: Breathe in short, forceful breaths; exhale strongly through each step without holding your breath for the whole push.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: bring each knee forward quickly to step again, keeping your feet moving under your hips rather than reaching.
steps.rom: Push for the set distance, typically 10-25 metres, maintaining the forward lean throughout.
steps.tempo: Keep a steady, powerful step cadence; heavy pushes are slower and grinding, light pushes faster and sprint-like.
steps.finish: Drive through the final step past the finish line before standing up.
steps.exit: Stand up, step away from the sled and walk back to recover; turn it around or walk around it to push back.

mistakes.m: Rounding the back and lowering the head
mistakes.fix: Keep a neutral spine with eyes looking a metre or two ahead.

mistakes.m: Taking long, slow strides
mistakes.fix: Use short, choppy steps to keep power on the turf.

mistakes.m: Bending the elbows and losing force
mistakes.fix: Lock the elbows so leg drive transfers into the sled.

mistakes.m: Loading too heavily and grinding to a halt
mistakes.fix: Reduce the load until you can keep moving for the whole distance.

safety: Clear the lane of people before each push, as you will be looking down.
Avoid holding your breath for the entire push; breathe in short bursts to limit blood pressure spikes.
Stop if you feel pain in the lower back, hamstrings or calves.
checks: Check the turf is dry and the lane is clear for the full distance.
Check plates are secure on the sled's posts.
Mark start and finish points.
reduceLoad: Reduce the load if you cannot keep moving, your back rounds, steps become stumbles, or you need far longer than planned to recover between pushes.
regressions: Light sled pushes at a walking pace

programming.frequency: 1-2 times per week, ideally away from heavy leg days
programming.initialLoad: Start with the empty sled or a light load and add plates until a 20-metre push takes about 10-15 seconds of hard effort.
programming.judgeLoad: The sled should move continuously; if you stall or your form breaks, the load is too heavy.
programming.progression: Add 10 kg or 5 metres of distance once all pushes are completed with good form, or shorten rest periods for conditioning.
programming.increase: Increase when you complete every push in the target time without stalling.
programming.maintain: Keep the load the same if your legs are still fatigued from lower-body training or if lower back discomfort appears.

name: Farmer's carries
musclesText: Primary: forearm flexors (grip), upper trapezius, trunk stabilisers. Secondary: obliques and quadratus lumborum, gluteus medius, quadriceps, rhomboids, calves, cardiovascular system.

steps.start: Stand between two heavy dumbbells or farmer's handles placed by the outside of your feet.
steps.setup: Choose dumbbells or handles of equal weight and clear a straight walkway of 15-30 metres or more.
steps.feet: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the handles centred beside each foot.
steps.grip: Grip each handle in the centre with a full, crushing grip and your thumb wrapped around; for farmer's handles, grip at the balance point.
steps.posture: Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to reach the handles with a flat back, then stand tall with shoulders down and back.
steps.brace: Brace your trunk as for a deadlift, ribs down, and keep it braced throughout the walk.
steps.initiate: Deadlift the weights up, pause to establish your posture, then take your first step.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: walk with short, controlled steps, heel to toe, keeping the weights still at your sides.
steps.breathing: Take short breaths behind your brace, exhaling partially and re-bracing every few steps rather than holding your breath throughout.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: at the end of the distance, turn with small steps or set the weights down before walking back.
steps.rom: Carry for the planned distance or time with arms straight and shoulders level the whole way.
steps.tempo: Walk at a steady, controlled pace; heavier loads require slower, shorter steps.
steps.finish: Stop walking with feet hip-width apart and stand tall for a moment.
steps.exit: Hinge and bend the knees to lower the weights to the floor beside your feet with a flat back; never drop them from standing height.

cues: Lift and lower like a deadlift

mistakes.m: Shrugging the shoulders up towards the ears
mistakes.fix: Keep shoulders down and back, with the traps working to hold them level.

mistakes.m: Leaning to one side or swaying
mistakes.fix: Use equal loads and brace your trunk; slow down.

mistakes.m: Rounding the back when picking up or setting down
mistakes.fix: Hinge at the hips with a flat back.

mistakes.m: Taking long strides that make the weights swing
mistakes.fix: Take short, controlled steps.

safety: Pick up and set down the weights with a flat back, as you would a deadlift.
Put the weights down under control as soon as your grip starts to fail; do not let them drop onto your feet.
Clear the walkway of people, kit and trip hazards.
checks: Check dumbbell heads or handle collars are secure.
Clear and measure the walking lane.
Use chalk if your hands are sweaty.
reduceLoad: Reduce the load if your posture leans or slumps, your grip fails before the planned distance, you shrug the shoulders up, or you feel lower back discomfort.
regressions: Lighter carry with a single kettlebell held in a goblet position

strength.rir: RPE 8-9; grip close to limit by the end

programming.frequency: 1-3 times per week
programming.initialLoad: Start with a load around 25-50% of your body weight in each hand that you can carry 20-30 metres with perfect posture.
programming.judgeLoad: Grip should be challenged by the end of each carry, but your posture and step rhythm must stay unchanged.
programming.progression: Add 2 kg per hand, or add 10 metres of distance, once all carries are completed with good posture.
programming.increase: Increase when you can complete every set with a steady stride and no need to set the weights down early.
programming.maintain: Keep the load the same if your grip or lower back is fatigued from earlier training or if you develop forearm or elbow discomfort.

name: Battle ropes
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system, anterior and lateral deltoids. Secondary: forearm flexors, biceps brachii, triceps brachii, trunk stabilisers, quadriceps and gluteus maximus (posture).

steps.start: Stand facing the anchor point, holding one end of the rope in each hand, with enough slack that the rope sags slightly.
steps.setup: Make sure the rope is anchored securely and lay it out straight; step back until there is a small amount of slack in the middle.
steps.feet: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees bent and hips back in a quarter-squat athletic stance.
steps.grip: Hold the rope ends with a neutral grip, thumbs on top, hands about hip-width apart in front of your hips.
steps.posture: Keep your chest up, back flat and a slight forward lean from the hips.
steps.brace: Brace your trunk firmly so the rope's pull does not twist you or round your back.
steps.initiate: Start the waves by lifting one hand to about shoulder height as the other drives down.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: alternate arms rapidly, driving each hand up and down from the shoulders to create continuous waves along the rope.
steps.breathing: Breathe rhythmically and quickly; avoid holding your breath as the intensity rises.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: as one arm drives down, the other lifts, so the action is continuous with no pause.
steps.rom: Move the hands between about hip height and shoulder height, so the waves travel all the way to the anchor.
steps.tempo: Work at a fast, steady rhythm for the interval, about 2-3 waves per second.
steps.finish: Finish the interval with the same wave quality you started with.
steps.exit: Lower the ropes to the floor, stand up and step away; lay the ropes straight for the next set.

mistakes.m: Standing too upright with straight legs
mistakes.fix: Bend the knees and sit the hips back into an athletic stance.

mistakes.m: Waves dying before the anchor
mistakes.fix: Use bigger arm movements and step back to remove excess slack.

mistakes.m: Rounding the back as you tire
mistakes.fix: Shorten the interval, brace harder and keep the chest up.

mistakes.m: Holding your breath
mistakes.fix: Breathe in a fast, steady rhythm throughout.

safety: Check the anchor point is secure before each session.
Keep a neutral spine; rounding forward under fatigue can strain the lower back.
Stop if you feel shoulder pain, especially with existing shoulder issues.
checks: Check the anchor and rope are free from fraying.
Clear a space around you and the rope.
Choose a rope weight and length suited to your level.
reduceLoad: Reduce the duration if the waves become small and irregular, your back rounds, or you feel shoulder discomfort.
regressions: Battle rope waves with shorter intervals

programming.frequency: 1-3 times per week
programming.initialLoad: Start with 6 rounds of 20 seconds of waves and 40 seconds of rest.
programming.judgeLoad: Wave height and rhythm should stay consistent through the entire interval; if they deteriorate early, shorten the work period.
programming.progression: Add 5 seconds to work periods, add rounds, or reduce rest.
programming.increase: Increase when you can keep consistent waves for all rounds.
programming.maintain: Keep the session the same if your shoulders or grip are fatigued from upper-body training, or reduce it if shoulder discomfort appears.

name: Low-impact interval training
musclesText: Primary: cardiovascular system. Secondary: quadriceps, gluteus maximus, gastrocnemius and soleus, iliopsoas, trunk stabilisers.

steps.start: Stand in a clear space with a timer set for your work and rest intervals and a short list of exercises ready.
steps.setup: Choose 4-6 moves with no jumping, such as alternating step-backs, squat to calf raise, high marches, standing knee drives, step jacks and boxer shuffles.
steps.feet: Begin each move with feet hip-width apart, toes pointing forward and weight spread across the whole foot.
steps.grip: Use your arms actively: swing them in rhythm with marches, reach overhead on step jacks or punch forward on boxer shuffles.
steps.posture: Stand tall with your chest up and head level; for squats, sit the hips back with a flat back.
steps.brace: Brace lightly through your trunk to keep your posture steady as you move quickly between exercises.
steps.initiate: Start each work interval at a moderate pace for the first few seconds, then build to your target effort.
steps.concentric: Effort phase: perform each move briskly for the work interval, for example 30-40 seconds, keeping one foot on the floor at all times.
steps.breathing: Breathe rhythmically, exhaling as you squat up, step or drive the knee; do not hold your breath.
steps.eccentric: Return phase: during the rest interval, march gently in place or walk while your breathing settles.
steps.rom: Use a comfortable range for each move, such as squatting to a depth you can control and stepping back only as far as you can balance.
steps.tempo: Use a work-to-rest ratio such as 30 seconds on and 30 seconds off, or 40 seconds on and 20 seconds off as fitness improves.
steps.finish: Complete 2-4 rounds of the circuit, then march slowly for 3-5 minutes to cool down.
steps.exit: Finish standing and walk around gently until your breathing returns to normal.

cues: One foot always on the floor

mistakes.m: Moving too slowly to raise your heart rate
mistakes.fix: Increase the pace and arm drive while keeping each move controlled.

mistakes.m: Losing form as you tire
mistakes.fix: Slow down slightly or reduce the range of motion to maintain posture.

mistakes.m: Knees caving in on squats and step-backs
mistakes.fix: Keep knees tracking over the toes.

mistakes.m: Holding your breath during effort
mistakes.fix: Exhale on the effort and breathe steadily throughout.

safety: Low-impact does not mean low-intensity; match the pace to your fitness and stop if you feel dizzy or unwell.
Use a chair or wall for balance on step-backs if your balance is limited.
Stop any move that causes joint pain and replace it with an easier option.
checks: Clear the space of trip hazards and check the floor is not slippery.
Set your interval timer and keep water nearby.
Wear supportive trainers.
reduceLoad: Reduce the pace or extend rest if you cannot speak a few words during work intervals, your form breaks down, or you feel joint pain or light-headedness.

endurance.rest: 20-30 s between moves; 1-2 min between rounds

programming.rehab: A gentle version with slower marches and shallow squats, using a chair for balance, can suit people returning to exercise; follow your physiotherapist's advice on which moves to include.
programming.frequency: 2-4 times per week
programming.initialLoad: Start with 2 rounds of 4 moves at 30 seconds of work and 30 seconds of rest.
programming.judgeLoad: You should be breathing hard by the end of each interval but able to say a few words, about RPE 6-8.
programming.progression: Add a round, lengthen work intervals by 5-10 seconds, or shorten rest periods, changing one at a time.
programming.increase: Increase when you complete all rounds with steady form and recover comfortably during the rests.
programming.maintain: Keep the session the same if you feel fatigued or sore from previous training, or reduce it if joint discomfort appears.
